content: An ACE inhibitor, such as enalapril (Vasotec/Renitec), ramipril (Altace/Tritace/Ramace/Ramiwin), quinapril (Accupril), perindopril (Coversyl/Aceon), lisinopril (Lisodur/Lopril/Novatec/Prinivil/Zestril), or benazepril (Lotensin), can be initiated in the management of heart failure. These medications improve symptoms and prognosis by mechanisms such as reducing afterload and promoting favorable ventricular remodeling. Common side effects include a dry cough and angioedema. Patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis or severe renal impairment are not suitable candidates for ACE inhibitors. After initiating diuresis, an ACE inhibitor like lisinopril can be started at a dose of 5 mg daily, with the dose titrated every 1–2 weeks to a target dose of 15–20 mg daily. ACE inhibitors are typically initiated before beta-blockers because they achieve hemodynamic effects more rapidly and are less likely to cause hemodynamic deterioration. Although some data suggest that aspirin may blunt the hemodynamic effects of ACE inhibitors, there is no evidence that aspirin reduces their clinical efficacy in heart failure patients. Aspirin should be given to patients with ischemic heart disease but avoided in those without it. If a patient cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor due to a persistent cough, an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) can be used as an alternative. ARBs block the activation of angiotensin II AT1 receptors, leading to vasodilation, reduced vasopressin secretion, and decreased production and secretion of aldosterone. Unlike ACE inhibitors, ARBs do not inhibit the breakdown of bradykinin, which makes them less likely to cause a persistent dry cough or angioedema. Commonly used ARBs in heart failure management include candesartan, valsartan, telmisartan, losartan, irbesartan, and olmesartan. The effectiveness of switching from an ACE inhibitor to an ARB was demonstrated in the CHARM-Alternative trial for candesartan. In general, ARBs are as effective or slightly less effective than ACE inhibitors in treating congestive heart failure. It is a class 2a recommendation to substitute an ARB for an ACE inhibitor if the patient is already taking an ARB for another indication. The addition of an ARB to an ACE inhibitor was assessed in the CHARM-Added trial, which showed a reduction in the composite primary endpoint but no reduction in mortality. The VALIANT trial demonstrated that adding an ARB to an ACE inhibitor in the post-MI setting is not recommended. In contrast, the EMPHASIS-HF trial showed that adding eplerenone (an aldosterone antagonist) to ACE inhibition improved clinical outcomes, including mortality, in patients with class II or III heart failure and reduced LVEF. Based on these findings, an aldosterone antagonist, rather than an ARB, should be added to an ACE inhibitor in patients with NYHA class II heart failure and LVEF <30%, post-MI patients with LVEF <40% and heart failure symptoms or diabetes, and patients with class III or IV heart failure and LVEF <35%. The combined use of an ACE inhibitor, ARB, and aldosterone antagonist (triple therapy) is relatively contraindicated. Beta-blockers are the third step in heart failure management. They reduce heart rate, thereby lowering myocardial energy expenditure, prolonging diastolic filling, and increasing the duration of coronary perfusion. Beta-blockers also mitigate the toxic effects of catecholamines on the myocardium. Once a stable dose of a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor has been achieved, one of the three beta-blockers shown to improve survival (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, or bisoprolol) can be added, with the dose titrated based on patient tolerance. Beta-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (e.g., pindolol or acebutolol) should be avoided. Meta-analyses have shown a 35% reduction in one-year mortality when beta-blockers are added to ACE inhibitors in heart failure. While there are no direct comparisons between beta-blockers, some data suggest that carvedilol may improve LVEF more than others but may be less well-tolerated due to its vasodilatory properties. Patients who have been over-diuresed may not tolerate the addition of a beta-blocker. Initiation of beta-blockers should be undertaken by individuals or centers specializing in heart failure management due to the potential for hemodynamic decompensation. Therapy should begin with very low doses, doubling every two weeks until the target dose is achieved or symptoms prevent further dose escalation. Patients should be informed that it may take 1–3 months for beta-blockers to improve heart failure symptoms. Aldosterone antagonists represent the fourth step in heart failure management and can be added to the regimen of select patients. These include patients with class II heart failure and LVEF <30%, class III/IV heart failure and LVEF <35%, or post-ST-segment elevation MI with LVEF <40% who have symptomatic heart failure or diabetes. Renal function and potassium levels must be carefully monitored in patients receiving aldosterone antagonists. Eplerenone has fewer endocrine side effects (1%) than spironolactone (10%) but is more expensive. A reasonable strategy is to initiate therapy with spironolactone at 25–50 mg daily and switch to eplerenone at 25–50 mg daily if endocrine side effects develop.
